content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a comprehensive operational handbook on tuberculosis (TB) treatment, specifically focusing on drug-resistant TB. This handbook serves as a practical guide to complement the latest WHO consolidated guidelines on TB treatment, including multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) and isoniazid-resistant TB (Hr-TB). It provides detailed recommendations for designing and implementing treatment regimens for these forms of TB, based on the most recent evidence and best practices. The handbook emphasizes the importance of drug susceptibility testing (DST) to guide treatment decisions. DST can be performed using molecular techniques to detect resistance-conferring mutations or phenotypic methods to assess drug susceptibility. Rapid molecular testing is particularly critical for detecting resistance to rifampicin and fluoroquinolones, as these results are essential for selecting the most appropriate initial treatment regimen. While DST for some drugs, such as ethambutol and pyrazinamide, is not yet widely available, the handbook underscores the need for national TB programs to build capacity for reliable DST and surveillance systems to monitor local patterns of drug resistance. The document also highlights the importance of patient-centered care, including informed consent, adherence support, and active monitoring for adverse events. Adverse events, which may occur during TB treatment, range from mild to severe and require careful management. Serious adverse events, such as life-threatening reactions or hospitalizations, necessitate immediate intervention, including discontinuation of the suspected drug if necessary. Treatment regimens for MDR/RR-TB are categorized as shorter or longer regimens. Shorter regimens last less than 12 months and are largely standardized, while longer regimens extend beyond 18 months and are tailored based on individual drug resistance patterns and patient history. Empiric treatment, initiated before laboratory confirmation of drug resistance, may be necessary in certain cases, such as when DST results are unavailable. However, the handbook stresses the importance of minimizing empiric treatment to avoid the risk of ineffective therapy and further resistance development. The handbook also addresses the use of off-label drugs in TB treatment. While some drugs, such as bedaquiline and delamanid, were initially used off-label, sufficient evidence has now been gathered to support their inclusion in TB regimens. Clinical judgment remains essential when using off-label drugs, particularly in cases where extended use beyond the approved duration may offer better outcomes for patients. For pediatric patients, obtaining DST results can be challenging due to difficulties in collecting adequate specimens. In such cases, treatment regimens are often based on the drug resistance patterns of the index case or local surveillance data. The handbook emphasizes the need for reliable clinical histories and population-level data to guide treatment decisions in the absence of individual DST results. Operational research is identified as a key component in improving TB treatment outcomes. This research aims to bridge the gap between clinical efficacy and real-world effectiveness, providing evidence to inform the adoption and integration of new interventions within health systems. The handbook encourages national TB programs to prioritize operational research to enhance program performance and patient outcomes. Finally, the handbook underscores the importance of safety monitoring, patient support, and management of comorbidities during TB treatment. Regular clinical and bacteriological follow-up is essential to assess treatment response and identify any adverse events. Social support mechanisms are also critical to ensuring patient adherence to treatment regimens. In settings where aDSM has not been fully implemented, healthcare providers are encouraged to establish appropriate monitoring schedules to safeguard patient safety and treatment success.
